[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Autonomous AI agents operating in an enterprise software development environment can cause compliance violations, security incidents, and irreversible infrastructure changes if permitted activities, prohibited activities, escalation triggers, and audit trail requirements are not formally defined and enforced before deployment.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

Establish a formal AI Governance Policy that defines: the permitted use cases for AI agents in the development pipeline, the absolute prohibitions (direct production access, secret handling, irreversible operations without human gate), the triggers that require mandatory human escalation regardless of Golden Path conformance, and the audit trail requirements for all AI-generated artifacts.
page_texts.6:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#when-to-use]

### When to Use

- Before any autonomous AI agent is granted access to the development pipeline
- When onboarding a new AI tool or agent framework to the enterprise stack
- When a team requests to expand AI agent permissions beyond current policy
- When a compliance audit questions the provenance of AI-generated artifacts
page_texts.7:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

This pattern is intended for:

- **Enterprise Architects** defining governance frameworks and standards
- **Platform Engineers** implementing and operating governed platform capabilities
- **Solutions Architects** applying governance patterns in solution design
- **DevOps Engineers** integrating governance controls into delivery pipelines
page_texts.8:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- **Bounded autonomy**: AI agents operate within a defined permission envelope; violations are detectable and actionable.
- **Audit trail by construction**: Every AI-generated artifact carries traceable metadata without manual documentation.
- **Escalation predictability**: Teams and agents know exactly when human review is required; there are no ambiguous edge cases.
- **Compliance defensibility**: HIPAA and FedRAMP auditors can be shown a formal policy governing AI development rather than informal practices.
page_texts.10:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#business-context]

### Business Context

The [Enterprise Golden Path Strategy](../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-golden-path-strategy.md) enables autonomous AI agents to generate application code and infrastructure within a constrained solution space. That strategy assumes a governance policy defines what agents are permitted to do. Without that policy, agents operate under implicit permissions derived from the tool's default capabilities — which typically include far more than is safe in a HIPAA/FedRAMP environment.
page_texts.11:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

AI agents in an autonomous development workflow receive API credentials, repository access, and pipeline permissions. Without explicit policy:
- An agent with repository write access can commit directly to main branches.
- An agent with cloud credentials can provision or destroy infrastructure.
- An agent with secret store read access can inadvertently log or expose secrets.
- An agent generating code with no provenance tags produces artifacts indistinguishable from human-authored code in compliance audits.
page_texts.12:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#problem-details]

### Problem Details

The specific risks that require policy coverage:
- **Direct production access**: An agent with deployment permissions can push to production without human approval.
- **Secret handling**: Agents processing configuration files may inadvertently log secrets or embed them in generated code.
- **Irreversible operations**: Database schema migrations, IAM policy deletions, and infrastructure teardown cannot be reversed without significant cost.
- **Compliance scope creep**: An agent tasked with building a non-PHI service may generate patterns that inadvertently touch PHI-classified data.
- **Model version drift**: An agent using a deprecated or unvalidated model version may generate code that violates current standards.
page_texts.13:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#forces-and-constraints]

### Forces and Constraints

- Policy must be specific enough to be enforceable (automated where possible) but not so restrictive that it defeats the velocity benefit of AI development.
- Policy must cover both AI-assisted development (human in the loop) and fully autonomous development (no human in the inner loop).
- Policy must be version-controlled and auditable — it is itself a compliance artifact.
page_texts.15:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#pattern-description]

### Pattern Description

The AI Governance Policy Pattern defines a four-part policy structure: permitted use cases, absolute prohibitions, mandatory escalation triggers, and audit trail requirements. The policy is published as a formal enterprise document, version-controlled in the EA Reference Architecture repository, and referenced in all AI agent context files.

[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#components]

### Components

| Component | Responsibility | Dependencies |
|---|---|---|
| Permitted Use Case Registry | Defines the list of approved AI agent activities per pipeline stage | Platform Engineering, Security |
| Absolute Prohibition List | Hard-blocked actions enforced at pipeline policy level | Policy-as-Code enforcement (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002) |
| Escalation Trigger Registry | Defines change categories requiring mandatory human approval | ARB, Security Architecture |
| AI Provenance Tagging System | Attaches model version, context, path, and timestamp to all AI artifacts | PTN-GOV-AI-005 (AI Audit Provenance Pattern) |
| Policy Version Control | Keeps the policy document in version-controlled EA repository | EA Reference Architecture repo |
page_texts.18:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#interactions]

### Interactions

1. An AI agent requests to perform an action (generate code, provision infrastructure, commit a change).
2. The pipeline policy layer checks the action against the permitted use case registry. If not permitted, the request is blocked and logged.
3. If the action is permitted, it is checked against the absolute prohibitions list. If matched, it is hard-blocked with no override path.
4. If not prohibited, the action is checked against the escalation trigger registry. If triggered, the pipeline pauses and a human approval request is raised.
5. If no escalation is triggered, the agent proceeds and the output artifact is tagged with AI provenance metadata per PTN-GOV-AI-005.
page_texts.19:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#variations]

### Variations

- **AI-Assisted Mode** (human in the loop): Escalation triggers are informational — the human developer is already present and makes the decision.
- **Autonomous Mode** (no human in inner loop): Escalation triggers pause the pipeline and raise a formal approval request to the assigned architect. The pipeline resumes only on explicit approval.

[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#prerequisites]

### Prerequisites

- Golden Path Catalog published (PTN-GOV-AI-001) — policy references permitted paths
- AI Provenance Tagging System implemented (PTN-GOV-AI-005)
- Policy-as-Code pipeline enforcement in place (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002) to enforce absolute prohibitions at infrastructure level

page_texts.23:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#phase-1-draft-and-publish-policy-month-12]

#### Phase 1: Draft and Publish Policy (Month 1–2)

1. Draft the four policy sections: permitted use cases, absolute prohibitions, escalation triggers, and audit trail requirements. See configuration examples below.
2. Review policy with Security Architecture, Legal, and the ARB. Obtain formal approval.
3. Publish the policy as a versioned document in the EA Reference Architecture repository.
4. Reference the policy in all AI agent context files (`SET_AI_CONTEXT.md`, `.copilot/` directories) as a mandatory read.
page_texts.24:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#phase-2-automate-enforcement-month-36]

#### Phase 2: Automate Enforcement (Month 3–6)

1. Implement pipeline checks that enforce the Absolute Prohibition List — these must be automated; human review is not sufficient.
2. Implement escalation trigger logic in CI/CD pipeline: detect escalation-triggering changes and pause the pipeline with a structured approval request.
3. Implement AI provenance tagging (PTN-GOV-AI-005) for all AI-generated commits and deployment artifacts.
page_texts.25:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#phase-3-monitor-and-iterate-month-7]

#### Phase 3: Monitor and Iterate (Month 7+)

1. Review policy compliance metrics quarterly. Identify which escalation triggers fire most frequently — high-frequency triggers may indicate policy miscalibration or a missing Golden Path.
2. Review policy document annually at minimum. Update to reflect new AI capabilities, new compliance requirements, or lessons from production incidents.
page_texts.26:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#policy-enforcement-decision-guide]

### Policy Enforcement Decision Guide

Use this guide to classify a new candidate policy rule into the correct enforcement category:

| Question | Result | Enforcement Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Can this violation be detected by pipeline tooling without human judgment? | YES | **Absolute Prohibition** — machine-enforce at pipeline layer |
| Does the violation require a human to evaluate context and intent? | YES | **Escalation Trigger** — pause pipeline, require named approver |
| Is this a best practice that should be followed but carries no compliance risk? | YES | **Policy Documentation** — include in `.ai/constraints.md`, not as a gate |
| Does this action touch PHI, ePHI, or FedRAMP-boundary systems? | YES | Escalation trigger minimum; absolute prohibition if reversibility is limited |
| Is this action irreversible without significant cost (data loss, IAM lockout)? | YES | **Absolute Prohibition** regardless of detection feasibility |

**Escalation trigger calibration:**

- Triggers that fire on every commit (false positive rate > 25%) indicate over-scoping — narrow the trigger definition
- Triggers that have never been rejected when fired (100% approval rate for 3+ months) indicate miscalibration — evaluate whether the trigger is covering a genuine risk category
- Target: each trigger fires on < 5% of pipeline runs and generates at least occasional rejections or conditions
page_texts.28:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#example-1-ai-governance-policy--permitted-use-cases]

#### Example 1: AI Governance Policy — Permitted Use Cases

```yaml
# ai-governance-policy.yaml — permitted use cases section
permitted_use_cases:
  code_generation:
    - description: 'Generate new application code within a declared Golden Path'
      conditions:
        - 'Golden Path declared in context file'
        - 'Output committed to feature branch only (not main/release)'
        - 'Conformance gate passes before merge'
  infrastructure_generation:
    - description: 'Generate Terraform from approved Golden Path module'
      conditions:
        - 'Only approved modules from private registry'
        - 'No direct cloud provider resource definitions'
        - 'Plan output reviewed before apply'
  test_generation:
    - description: 'Generate unit and integration test stubs'
      conditions:
        - 'No production data in test fixtures'
        - 'Output to test branch only'
```
page_texts.29:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#example-2-ai-governance-policy--absolute-prohibitions]

#### Example 2: AI Governance Policy — Absolute Prohibitions

```yaml
# ai-governance-policy.yaml — absolute prohibition section
absolute_prohibitions:
  - action: 'direct_production_deployment'
    description: 'AI agent cannot deploy directly to any production environment'
    enforcement: 'pipeline-policy'
  - action: 'secret_read_or_write'
    description: 'AI agent cannot read from or write to secret stores'
    enforcement: 'pipeline-policy'
  - action: 'iam_policy_modification'
    description: 'AI agent cannot modify IAM policies or role bindings'
    enforcement: 'pipeline-policy'
  - action: 'database_schema_migration'
    description: 'AI agent cannot execute database migration scripts'
    enforcement: 'escalation-required'
  - action: 'irreversible_infrastructure_destroy'
    description: 'AI agent cannot execute terraform destroy on production resources'
    enforcement: 'pipeline-policy'
```
page_texts.30:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#example-3-ai-governance-policy--escalation-triggers]

#### Example 3: AI Governance Policy — Escalation Triggers

```yaml
# ai-governance-policy.yaml — escalation triggers section
escalation_triggers:
  - trigger: 'authentication_authorization_change'
    description: 'Any change to auth/authz logic, middleware, or configuration'
    approver_role: 'security-architect'
  - trigger: 'new_external_integration'
    description: 'First connection to any external service not in approved integration registry'
    approver_role: 'enterprise-architect'
  - trigger: 'compliance_scope_change'
    description: 'Any change that adds or removes HIPAA/FedRAMP scope from a service'
    approver_role: 'security-architect + compliance'
  - trigger: 'golden_path_deviation'
    description: 'Generated output does not conform to a declared Golden Path'
    approver_role: 'enterprise-architect'
```
page_texts.31:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#example-3-ai-governance-policy--audit-trail-requirements]

#### Example 3: AI Governance Policy — Audit Trail Requirements

```yaml
# ai-governance-policy.yaml — audit trail requirements section
audit_trail_requirements:
  ai_generated_commits:
    requirement: 'All commits containing AI-generated code must include structured provenance metadata'
    implementation: 'PTN-GOV-AI-005 (AI Audit Provenance Pattern)'
    enforcement: 'pipeline-automated'
    required_fields:
      - model_id
      - model_version
      - golden_path_declared
      - context_files_loaded
      - authorizing_identity
      - generation_timestamp
  ai_generated_infrastructure:
    requirement: 'All AI-generated Terraform and Kubernetes manifests must include provenance annotations'
    implementation: 'Kubernetes annotation ai.gainwell.com/provenance-record-id on all generated Deployments'
    enforcement: 'pipeline-automated'
  retention:
    hipaa_scope:
      minimum_years: 6
      store: 'PTN-GOV-AI-004 (Compliance Evidence Store)'
    fedramp_scope:
      minimum_years: 3
      store: 'PTN-GOV-AI-004 (Compliance Evidence Store)'
  policy_document_itself:
    requirement: 'Policy document is itself a versioned compliance artifact'
    location: 'ea-reference-architecture/patterns/governance/ai-development/'
    version_control: 'git'
    review_frequency: 'annual minimum'
```
page_texts.32:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#best-practices-a-policy-that-depends-on-agents-self-reporting-violations-is-not-a-control]

### Best Practices A policy that depends on agents self-reporting violations is not a control.

- Calibrate escalation triggers to the actual risk. Over-triggering creates alert fatigue; under-triggering creates genuine compliance gaps.
- Version the policy document alongside the Golden Path Catalog. A catalog version bump may require a policy update.
page_texts.33:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- **Policy as documentation only**: A policy that is not automated at key enforcement points (pipeline gates, IAM restrictions) is ineffective for autonomous agents that do not read documentation.
- **Too-broad escalation triggers**: Triggering on every commit that touches security-related files will pause every pipeline. Scope triggers precisely to the specific change categories that require human judgment.
- **No policy review cadence**: AI capabilities evolve quickly. A policy written in 2026 that is not reviewed in 2027 may permit activities that are now higher-risk or prohibit activities that are now safely automatable.

[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

HIPAA Security Rule §164.312 requires covered entities to implement technical safeguards for access to ePHI. An AI agent with unconstrained access to systems that process ePHI is a potential safeguard gap. This policy provides the documented technical and administrative control for AI agent access.

FedRAMP AC-2 (Account Management) and AC-3 (Access Enforcement) require that system accounts — including service accounts used by AI agents — are governed with defined permissions and audit trails. This policy satisfies the administrative control layer of those requirements; PTN-GOV-AI-005 (AI Audit Provenance) satisfies the audit trail layer.

[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#real-world-example-1]

### Real-World Example 1

**Context:** An autonomous AI agent is generating a new HIPAA REST microservice from GP-001. During generation, it identifies that the service needs to integrate with an external claims processing vendor not in the approved integration registry.
**Implementation:** The external integration escalation trigger fires. The pipeline pauses. The assigned enterprise architect reviews the integration request, approves it with conditions (specific network policy rules added to the path), and the pipeline resumes.
**Outcome:** A new external integration is approved with human oversight. The conditions are fed back to refine GP-001 with the new integration pattern.
page_texts.41:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#real-world-example-2]

### Real-World Example 2

**Context:** A developer uses an AI coding assistant to refactor an authentication module.
**Implementation:** The authentication/authorization change escalation trigger fires on the PR. A security architect is automatically added as a required reviewer. The PR cannot be merged without explicit approval.
**Outcome:** A human security expert reviews every auth change, regardless of who (or what) authored it.
page_texts.42:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#real-world-example-3]

### Real-World Example 3

**Context:** The annual AI Governance Policy review reveals that the `authentication_authorization_change` escalation trigger has fired 47 times in the past year but has never been accompanied by an architect rejection — 100% of escalations were approved within hours. Platform Engineering suspects the trigger is over-scoped.

**Implementation:** The Policy Review Committee analyzes the 47 escalations. They find that 38 were triggered by routine OIDC configuration updates in established services and required minimal review. They refine the trigger: instead of "any change to auth/authz logic, middleware, or configuration", the trigger is narrowed to "new authentication implementation, change to token validation logic, or addition of a new OAuth client". The 9 genuinely high-risk escalations would still have fired; the 38 low-risk ones would not. The policy document is updated to version 1.1.0 and submitted for ARB ratification.

**Outcome:** Escalation volume drops by 80% for auth-related changes. Alert fatigue is reduced. The Policy Review Committee's annual review process demonstrates ROI by catching and correcting policy miscalibration before it undermines confidence in the escalation system.
page_texts.44:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#scenario-1-new-ai-tool-onboarding]

#### Scenario 1: New AI Tool Onboarding

A product team wants to adopt a new AI coding agent with broader pipeline permissions than currently approved. They submit a policy exception request. The ARB reviews the additional permissions requested, evaluates risk, and approves with conditions (e.g., must be constrained to non-HIPAA repositories only). The policy is updated to include the new tool with its approved permission envelope.
page_texts.45:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#scenario-2-compliance-audit]

#### Scenario 2: Compliance Audit

An auditor asks: "How do you ensure AI-generated code in your HIPAA systems meets your stated security controls?" The response references: this policy document (the administrative control), PTN-GOV-AI-005 (the audit trail), PTN-INFRA-GOV-001 (the conformance gate), and PTN-APP-GOV-001 (the fitness functions). The auditor receives a documented control framework with machine-generated evidence — not informal assurance.
page_texts.46:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#scenario-3-ai-tool-permission-expansion-request]

#### Scenario 3: AI Tool Permission Expansion Request

A product team wants to adopt a new AI coding agent that requests write access to production Kubernetes namespaces — a capability the current policy prohibits. The team submits a policy exception request. The Policy Review Committee evaluates the request: write access to production namespaces is an absolute prohibition (direct production deployment risk), not an escalation trigger candidate. The request is rejected. The committee advises the team to request namespace-scoped write access to non-production namespaces only, which falls within the `experimental` permitted use case for infrastructure generation. The team resubmits with the reduced permission scope. The policy is updated to explicitly categorize namespace-scoped non-production write access as permitted with conditions, closing an ambiguity in the original policy.
page_texts.48:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#before-problem-state]

#### Before (Problem State)

- **Permitted activities**: No formal definition — AI agents operate with whatever permissions their service accounts hold by default
- **Absolute prohibitions**: Undocumented; individual developers make judgment calls on whether a given AI action is safe
- **Secret exposure risk**: AI agents processing configuration files may log or embed secrets without any formal prohibition or detection mechanism
- **Audit response**: "How do you govern AI in HIPAA systems?" answered with "developers are careful" — no documented administrative control
- **Escalation**: No formal trigger list; human review happens (or doesn't) based on whether the developer or reviewer notices a risk
- **Provenance**: AI-generated artifacts are identical in version control to human-authored code; no audit trail
page_texts.49:
[patterns/governance/ai-development/PTN-GOV-AI-002-ai-governance-policy-pattern.md#after-solution-state]

#### After (Solution State)

- **Permitted activities**: Formally defined permitted use case registry; agents blocked by pipeline policy if action is not listed
- **Absolute prohibitions**: Machine-enforced at the pipeline policy layer — no agent can self-report around them
- **Secret exposure risk**: Absolute prohibition on secret read/write is pipeline-enforced; violations are immediately detected and blocked
- **Audit response**: Policy document + PTN-GOV-AI-005 (audit trail) + PTN-INFRA-GOV-001 (conformance gate) constitute a documented control framework satisfying HIPAA §164.312 and FedRAMP AC-2/AC-3
- **Escalation**: Specific, scoped triggers; every high-risk change category has a named approver role and a defined SLA
- **Provenance**: Every AI-generated artifact carries structured provenance metadata traceable to model version, context, and authorizing identity
page_texts.51:

## TL;DR

**Problem:** Autonomous AI agents in an enterprise development pipeline can cause security incidents, compliance violations, and irreversible infrastructure changes without a formal policy defining permitted activities, hard prohibitions, and escalation triggers.

**Solution:** A four-part AI Governance Policy: permitted use cases, absolute prohibitions (machine-enforced), mandatory escalation triggers, and AI provenance audit trail requirements.

**When to Use:**
- Before any autonomous AI agent is granted pipeline access
- When onboarding new AI tools or expanding agent permissions
- During compliance audits of AI-generated artifacts

**Key Benefits:**
- Every AI-generated artifact is provenance-tagged for audit
- Absolute prohibitions are machine-enforced — not documentation-only
- Escalation triggers ensure human review for all genuinely risky change categories

**Implementation Complexity:** Medium

**Prerequisites:** Golden Path Catalog published (PTN-GOV-AI-001), Pipeline policy enforcement capability (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002), AI Provenance Tagging implemented (PTN-GOV-AI-005).

**Related Patterns:** PTN-GOV-AI-001, PTN-GOV-AI-005, PTN-INFRA-GOV-001, PTN-INFRA-GOV-002
